title: Primordium: Spore-like Evolution Game, Now Aquatic Stage Included!
author: Ouvolk
selftext:
Hi all. I'm developing Primordium, an evolution sandbox I'm building in Godot.

You start as a single cell in a tide pool: eat, or get eaten by something bigger. Between generations you rebuild your cell in an editor, and every part changes how it swims and fights. Then you grow into a swimmer on a reef, add fins, gills or a lure, and at some point you choose: walk out onto land, or stay in the sea and found your tribe under water.

\*\*The free demo is the whole cell stage\*\*, about half an hour: [https://akinjigames.itch.io/primordium](https://akinjigames.itch.io/primordium)

There, You can find more gifs and screenshots for other stages as well.

I have also a kickstarter campaign launching soon, follow it if you are interested: [https://www.kickstarter.com/projects/primordium/primordium-evolve-your-own-creature-from-a-single-cell](https://www.kickstarter.com/projects/primordium/primordium-evolve-your-own-creature-from-a-single-cell)

You can play it right in the browser, but the game is made to be downloaded. The Windows and macOS builds look and run better, and the browser version can load slowly.

The later stages (sea, creature editor, island, tribe) are already playable but in the development build, not in the demo yet.  
It's pre-alpha, so expect rough edges. I'd really like to hear your feedback and ideas. I am always reading the comments and actually add/change something when it makes sense.

I am using Claude mainly.

**How the work is split**

* One strong model acts as the lead: it plans, writes briefs, reviews, and does some of the work itself.
* Cheaper models get the bulk coding as subagents, each in its own git worktree so they don’t overwrite each other.
* I mix several providers and route by task: the simplest jobs go to the cheapest model, and the expensive one is only used when the others fail.

**What made it work**

* **Everything is procedural.** There are no imported 3D models in the project. Creatures, plants, villages and effects are built by code, with 127 shaders. That is what lets an AI change the look of the game at all, and it’s also why the editors can reshape everything.
* **Tests and bots.** About 95 test files; the cell stage alone runs over 2,100 checks. Bots play the stages for 30 to 60 game minutes to find where a path breaks or gets boring.
* **Steps need to be checked.** Every visual change is recorded from the running game and checked frame by frame. A lot of “done” turned out not to be done when someone finally looked.
* **Written memory.** A handover file and a set of standing rules carry decisions between sessions if I switch to something else.
